surface_forms: la de moins en moins existante Mlle Simonet
Une jeune blonde, seule, à l'air triste

appraisal_events.evidence: Les femmes de Rivebelle chuchotent : « Quel joli garçon ! Moi je le trouve épatant ; et quel chic ! ... on se jetterait au feu pour un homme comme ça » ; son indifférence à toute femme qui n'est pas son actrice « lui donnait aux yeux de celles-ci un prestige singulier » ; et le narrateur y ajoute son propre portrait admiratif de « l'architecture féodale » et de la tête en donjon.
appraisal_events.explanation: The demi-monde women openly admire Saint-Loup's looks, chic and constancy, and his fidelity to his mistress is said to give him a singular prestige among them; the narrator does not ironize this but corroborates it with his own elevating feudal-architecture portrait. Their contempt for his mistress only sharpens the contrast in his favor.

appraisal_events.evidence: « une sorte d'ataxie morale » ; « je serais mort contre elle, je me serais laissé massacrer sans offrir de défense, sans bouger, abeille engourdie par la fumée du tabac » ; grand-mère, travail et livres ne sont plus vus que « dans un lointain sans réalité » ; « Presque toutes étaient connues, à défaut de moi, par Saint-Loup » et « J'aurais voulu qu'il me présentât à ces femmes ».
appraisal_events.explanation: The narrator's retrospective analysis diagnoses his intoxicated evening as passivity, loss of self-governance and dependence on others, and stages him comparatively as the one who lacks the acquaintance and access that Saint-Loup possesses. The exceptional pleasure he reports is explicitly framed as the very thing that disarms him, so the dominant movement is diminishing.

status_effects.explanation: Saint-Loup is clearly elevated: admired aloud by the women of Rivebelle for his looks, chic and constancy, credited with a singular prestige, and then monumentalized by the narrator's own portrait.

He is shown as emotionally passive and captive to the present, receiving his states from others, indifferent to danger and to everything he loves, which locally weakens rather than strengthens his position.
Within the Rivebelle milieu he is the unknown one, dependent on Saint-Loup both for company and for introductions to women who all already know his friend.

Under the same intoxicated devaluation, Mlle Simonet and her friends fall into insignificance: knowing her becomes easy but indifferent, and every unknown woman seems a thousand times more desirable than the increasingly non-existent Mlle Simonet.

ambiguities: Albertine's local erasure is explicitly framed by the narrator as an artefact of drunkenness that will reverse the next day (« Les personnes qui n'avaient plus d'importance ... reprendront le lendemain leur densité »), so the diminishment is real within the passage but marked as temporary and subjective rather than a settled devaluation.

The « d'Orléans » invoked by the woman as Saint-Loup's inseparable companion is a bare name with no referent fixed by the passage or the reference sheet; he functions as a prestige anchor for Saint-Loup but cannot be resolved to a known entity.
